team
BoilGuard is a solo entry by Shermaine Yap Shi Min, a computing student at Asia Pacific University in Malaysia, for the OpenCV AI Competition 2026, powered by AWS.
problem

Cooking is the leading cause of home fires, and unattended cooking is by far the leading factor. In Malaysia, firefighters sum it up in three words: lalai, lupa, leka. Negligence, forgetting, distraction.
lag

A boil-over is the everyday version. Milk foams over within seconds, and turning the knob then is too late: an electric hob keeps heating for four to eight seconds. A warning has to come before that lag runs out.
idea
BoilGuard is a camera above the stove. It finds the pot rim, measures the foam in millimetres, forecasts when it will spill, and acts early enough to beat the heat lag.
demo1

This is the live app, running on AWS Lambda. I choose milk on a ceramic hob, with the cook away. Each run simulates sixty seconds of boiling, and the full OpenCV pipeline, forecaster and agent run in the cloud.
demo2
Here is the camera view annotated by OpenCV. The cyan ellipse is the detected rim, the dotted line is the foam front, and the panel shows the distance to the rim, the forecast, and every action.
demo3

The measurement tracks the truth. When steam hides the pot, the agent turns on the hood fan to see better. When a spill within the heat lag becomes likely, it alerts the cook, turns the heat down through AWS IoT Core, and checks from the video that the foam is falling. Amazon Bedrock writes the messages from the numbers only.
vision

Perception is classical OpenCV five, with no training data. Canny, contours and fitEllipse find the rim. A polar remap unwraps the pot, so rising foam becomes a front moving outward. Phase correlation cancels shake, a dehazing model sees through steam, and a change-point search finds the front against the static pot wall. All in under twenty milliseconds per frame.
predict

Foam grows exponentially, then saturates. An OpenCV Kalman filter tracks that growth, and Monte Carlo sampling gives the chance of spilling before a heat change can take effect. The agent perceives, decides, acts and verifies, with three levels of human control.
aws
One SAM template deploys a Lambda container, an IoT Core command topic with an S3 audit rule, SNS alerts, Bedrock, and CloudWatch metrics and alarms. GitHub Actions tests, deploys and smoke-tests it.
results

I tuned on a separate dev set and tested on sixty held-out scenes. With no system, every overflow-prone pot spilled. A rim alarm with the cook nearby still let eighty-eight percent spill, and BoilGuard's warnings alone let eighty percent spill: heat lag plus reaction time is too slow. Acting automatically, BoilGuard prevented all forty, with one unneeded heat cut on fourteen safe pots.
limits

The surface is measured to about three millimetres, and the spill is forecast within about a second at five seconds out. Limits: dark soups fooled rim detection in three of sixty scenes, it warns on some simmers, and all results are simulated. A real-stove study is next.
responsible
Only the pot is analysed, Bedrock sees numbers, not images, every command is audited, and BoilGuard only ever turns the heat down. Turning it back up is always the cook's decision.
close
BoilGuard. See it coming. Turn it down.
